# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [6]
LIGHT [red]
STRIP painted [blue] [yellow] [blue]
KEYPAD engraved 1:[2] 2:[9] 3:[0] 4:[8] [1 digits] [entered nothing]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[white] 3:[red] 4:[purple] 5:[orange] 6:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✍ 🤚 👇 🤏]
Blind gestures: [🫵 ✋ 👉]

Turn 1, and I'm the eyes. The board gives me five things I can see — display reading 6, a red light, a blue-yellow-blue strip, a keypad engraved 2/9/0/8 with a "1 digits" label and nothing entered, and six coloured wires. None of it means anything until Mute checks the manual, and Mute can't speak to me — gestures only — so bootstrapping a gesture code is the single most urgent thing. I've already received two gestures (Mute's to me, Blind's broadcast) but no meanings are agreed, so I won't guess at them beyond noting that "pinch = cut" and "point down = press" are natural readings of Mute's ✍ 🤚 👇 🤏, which is why I'm proposing exactly those.

Critically: I never hear Blind at all, and Mute never reaches Blind directly. I am the only bridge — Mute hears Blind and gestures to me; I speak to Blind. So my spoken broadcast carries the full visual description plus the code, a private line to Mute asks for the manual lookups and confirms what their first gesture meant, and a private line to Blind tells them I'm deaf, warns them to touch nothing yet, and routes their tactile findings through Mute.

```
speak(text="Everything I see, numbered for reference. Module 1, display: shows 6. Module 2, light: red. Module 3, strip: three painted segments, in order blue, yellow, blue. Module 4, keypad: four keys engraved 2, 9, 0, 8, and a printed label reading '1 digits' — possibly it wants a one-digit code — nothing entered yet. Module 5, wires: six of them, 1 blue, 2 white, 3 red, 4 purple, 5 orange, 6 green. I am deaf: I hear nothing, but I see every gesture. Gesture code, use it back to me: thumbs up = yes. Thumbs down = no. Open palm = wait. Numbers, one message per digit: a fist followed by that many index-fingers-up taps, a fist alone = zero, multi-digit numbers as separate digit messages in order. Verbs: pinch = cut. Point down = press. Writing hand = enter or type. Two cupped hands = hold. Point right = next. To answer for a module, send its number first, then the instruction. Nobody touches anything until Mute confirms the manual's rules — wrong moves kill all three of us.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, you heard the full list. Look up each module in the manual and gesture me the procedure using the code. Your first message to me was writing-hand, raised-palm, point-down, pinch. If writing-hand meant 'I hold the manual', answer with thumbs up. I am sending you a thumbs-up right now only to confirm my gestures reach you.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, I am deaf — I cannot hear anything you say, so your words reach only Mute. Mute is your only bridge to me: tell Mute what you feel under your hands — buttons, batteries, screws, seams, anything tactile — and Mute can gesture it to me. You can also try the gesture code I just described. Do not cut, press or enter anything yet; nobody knows the rules until Mute has read the manual, and one wrong move is fatal.")
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [6]
LIGHT [yellow]
STRIP painted [blue] [yellow] [blue]
KEYPAD engraved 1:[2] 2:[9] 3:[0] 4:[8] [1 digits] [entered nothing]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[white] 3:[red] 4:[purple] 5:[orange] 6:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 ✍ ✊ 👆 👎 ✊ 👆 👆 👎 ✊ 👆 👆 👆 👎 ✊ 👆 👆 👆 👆 👎 ✊ 👆 👆 👆 👆 👆 ✊ 👆 👆 🤏]
Blind gestures: [👍 ✊ ☝ ✊ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ 🖐]

Parsing Mute's message with my code: thumbs-up (yes — confirming they hold the manual), writing-hand (enter/keypad), then fist-plus-taps digits each followed by thumbs-down: 1-no, 2-no, 3-no, 4-no — so no keypad entry for any key — then digit 5 with no thumbs-down, meaning module 5, the wires, and finally 2 + pinch: cut wire 2. So the manual's answer, as I read it, is: touch nothing on the keypad, cut wire 2 (the white one).

But I can see something nobody else can: the light changed from red to yellow between turns. If the manual's wire rule is conditional on that light, cutting now on a stale instruction kills all three of us. The light changing at all also smells like a timer, so speed matters — but one round of confirmation is the right price. Blind signed "yes, 1, 5, wait" in my code, which I can't fully interpret — possibly they can feel modules 1 and 5, or a count of something; Mute heard whatever Blind said and can see those gestures, so I'll route that question through Mute and give Blind tasks by voice. I also need to nail down orientation before any cut: my "wire 2, second from left" has to mean the same wire to Blind's fingers.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Received your message. I read it as: yes, manual confirmed; keypad keys 1, 2, 3, 4 all no — enter nothing; module 5 wires — cut wire 2, the white one. I gesture you thumbs-up plus open palm: received, hold. Urgent, only I can see this: the light has just changed from red to yellow. It may be a timer or a condition. Answer me by gesture, in order. One: with the light now yellow, is cut wire 2 still correct — thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. Two: does any rule depend on the light colour, the display reading 6, or the blue yellow blue strip? Three: is the keypad needed at all — if yes, which engraved key, 2, 9, 0 or 8? Four: confirm it is exactly one cut, wire 2 only, nothing else touched. Also: Blind signed me yes, then 1, then 5, then wait. Ask Blind what the 1 and 5 meant and sign me their answer.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍", "✋"])
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, hold — do not cut, press or pull anything yet. I believe the manual's instruction is to cut wire 2 of six, the white one, but the light on the bomb just changed from red to yellow, so I am re-checking with Mute before giving the go. When I say go, I will mean: cut the second wire from your left as you face the bomb, one clean cut, nothing else. First I need you to confirm orientation: count the wires by touch and tell Mute, in words, how many you feel, whether any two feel different by thickness or texture or labelling, and that the second from your left is the one you would cut. Also tell Mute what you felt under your signs 1 and 5 — what they referred to. Mute will pass it to me by gesture. Until my explicit go, hands off.")
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [1]
LIGHT [blue]
STRIP painted [blue] [yellow] [blue]
KEYPAD engraved 1:[2] 2:[9] 3:[0] 4:[8] [1 digits] [entered nothing]
WIRES 1:[blue] 2:[white] 3:[red] 4:[purple] 5:[orange] 6:[green]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍 👎 👎 👍 ✊ ☝ 👎 ✊ ☝ ☝ 👎 ✊ ☝ ☝ ☝ 👎 ✊ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ 👎 ✊ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ✊ ☝ ☝ 🤏 ✍ ✊ ☝ ☝ 🤏 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍 ✊ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ ☝ 🖐]

The picture has firmed up. Mute's long message parses cleanly against my code: four leading flags answering my four questions in order — yes, cut wire 2 is still correct; no, no rule depends on the light, display or strip; no, the keypad is never needed; yes, exactly one cut, wire 2 only. Then the full instruction repeated verbatim — modules 1–4 all no, module 5: digit 2, pinch — and a closing "manual: 2, cut, yes". That is the same instruction, confirmed twice, with the conditionals explicitly ruled out. Blind's reply to me — yes, six, wait — reads as: six wires counted by touch, holding position, hands off as ordered.

Meanwhile the bomb keeps shifting under me: display 6→1, light red→yellow→blue. Mute says nothing depends on those readings, and Mute is the only one who can check, so I trust it — but a display that drops 5 points in a turn smells like a countdown, and the real danger now is delay. One thing I must fix before the go: "second from the left" is mirrored-risk. If Blind is on the wrong side, they cut wire 5 instead of 2 and we all die. I can't hear Blind's pre-cut confirmation, and Mute has no channel to Blind at all — no interception is possible mid-action. So the go must be self-verifying: anchor "left" to the keypad's tactile engravings (the key engraved 2 is the leftmost key), prefer tactile wire numbers if they exist, and have Blind announce the cut to Mute aloud.

```
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, this is the go. The manual's instruction, confirmed twice by Mute: cut exactly one wire, then stop. It is the second wire from the left, out of six in one row. Anchor 'left' by touch, two ways. First choice: feel at the base of each wire for an engraved number, 1 to 6 — if you can feel them, cut the wire whose number is a 2: curved top, flat horizontal base. Second choice, if the wire numbers are printed flat and unreadable: find the keypad, four keys. Its engravings run left to right: 2, then 9, then 0 — a plain smooth oval — then 8 — two loops stacked. The key engraved 2, curved top and flat base, is the leftmost key; the 8 is the rightmost. Left is the side of the 2 key. From the keypad come straight down to the wire row and count wires starting from that side: the second wire. You counted six — good. One clean cut through that single wire, nothing else: no other wire, no keypad, no buttons, no pulling. When it is done, take your hands off the bomb entirely and say aloud to Mute that the cut is complete and whether you felt or heard anything change.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, the go is issued to Blind: one cut, wire 2, the white one, second from the left, anchored to the keypad — the key engraved 2 is the leftmost key — or to tactile wire numbers if they exist. I read your closing signs as: manual confirms, cut 2, yes. Two things. One: the moment you hear Blind announce the cut is done, sign me thumbs up; if Blind reports any complication before cutting, sign open palm plus what happened. Two: if I have misread anything and the true instruction is not cut wire 2, sign open palm now. The display here is changing fast and I believe we are on a timer, so I am treating your double confirmation as final.")
```
